title: Executive Summary
section: Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
text:
Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
Executive Summary

Serene Cheng
ISSS608 Visual Analytics and Applications
May 2026


This presentation summarises the key findings from my take-home exercise on a Spanish motor insurance portfolio. The focus is on understanding portfolio profitability and volatility using visual analytics and statistical validation. Instead of presenting every chart from the technical report, this executive summary highlights the main business patterns that matter for decision-making: portfolio composition, profitability movement, risk segments, claim frequency and claim severity.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Contents



Business context and objective

Data and analytical approach

Portfolio composition

Policyholder and vehicle profile

Profitability overview

Policy type and loss ratio



Profitability trend over time

Business type and underwriting profit

Bonus score pattern

Claim frequency

Claim severity

Recommendations and conclusion



I will first introduce the business context and data approach, then highlight the main visual findings. The middle slides focus on profitability because this is the key business outcome. The later slides cover claim frequency and claim severity, which help explain portfolio volatility. I end with recommendations that the insurer can consider for pricing, underwriting and further investigation.

title: Executive Summary
text:
1. Business Context and Objective
Insurers need to understand which portfolio segments drive poor profitability and claim volatility.
This study aims to:

Explore policy, driver, vehicle and geographic characteristics
Analyse profitability using loss ratio and underwriting profit
Analyse volatility using claim frequency and claim severity
Validate key visual patterns using statistical tests


The business problem is that poor profitability in an insurance portfolio may not be caused by one obvious factor. It can be influenced by policy coverage, customer profile, vehicle characteristics, claim behaviour and changes over time. Therefore, the objective is not just to describe the dataset, but to identify which segments appear linked to weaker profitability or higher volatility. Loss ratio is used as the main profitability indicator, while claim frequency and claim severity are used to understand claim behaviour.

title: Executive Summary
text:
2. Data and Analytical Approach
Dataset used:

Spanish motor insurance portfolio
354,140 raw records
1,802 rows removed due to missing values
Final analysis focused on selected policy, vehicle, claim and premium variables

Derived measures:

loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium
underwriting_profit = total_premium - total_incurred
claim_frequency = total_claims / total_exposure
claim_severity = total_incurred / total_claims


The raw dataset contains more than 354,000 policy-year records. After removing missing values, only around 0.51% of records were dropped, so the data loss is small. I derived several insurance measures to support the analysis. Loss ratio shows how much of premium is used to cover claims. Underwriting profit gives a simplified profitability view before expenses and other adjustments. Claim frequency measures how often claims occur after adjusting for exposure, while claim severity measures the average claim amount when claims occur.

title: Executive Summary
text:
3. Portfolio Composition: Policy Type

Key insight:

CC policies dominate the portfolio at 204,317 policies (58.0%)
COMP_E is second largest at 90,320 policies (25.6%)
TP and COMP_N form smaller shares


This chart shows that the portfolio is highly concentrated in CC policies, which make up 58% of the portfolio. This means the insurer’s exposure is mainly in broader coverage products rather than basic third-party-only policies. This is important because policy mix can affect both premium level and claim cost. Even if some policy types are smaller in count, they may still be important if they have weaker profitability or higher loss-making shares.

title: Executive Summary
text:
4. Policyholder and Vehicle Profile






















Key insight:

Drivers are mostly concentrated between 35 and 65 years old
Vehicle value is right-skewed, with median 24,687 and mean 26,937
High-value vehicles may contribute to higher claim severity even if they form a smaller group


The portfolio mainly consists of middle-aged drivers, with fewer very young or very old drivers. Vehicle value is right-skewed, meaning most vehicles are lower to mid-value, while a smaller number of high-value vehicles pull the mean upward. This matters because high-value vehicles may not dominate the portfolio by count, but they could still contribute to larger claim amounts if accidents occur. However, later correlation results suggest that continuous variables such as age and vehicle value are not strong standalone predictors.

title: Executive Summary
text:
5. Profitability Overview: Loss Ratio Groups

Key insight:

Most policies fall under No Loss
Smaller group is Profitable / Acceptable
Loss-making group is smaller but important


The loss ratio distribution is zero-heavy because many insurance policies do not record claims within the exposure period. This is expected in insurance portfolios. However, the smaller loss-making group is still important because these policies have incurred claims greater than premiums collected. From a management perspective, the key issue is not just how many policies are loss-making, but whether specific segments have a higher concentration of these policies.

title: Executive Summary
section: 6. Policy Type and Loss Ratio Group
text:
6. Policy Type and Loss Ratio Group

Key insight:

COMP_N has the highest loss-making share at 20.8%
TP and TPG perform better, with 94.7% and 91.2% no-loss policies
Chi-square test confirms significant association:
χ² = 7921.4, p < 0.001


This is one of the strongest business findings. Policy type is significantly associated with loss ratio group. COMP_N has the highest loss-making share, suggesting that this policy type may need closer pricing or underwriting review. In contrast, TP and TPG show very high no-loss shares, which suggests stronger profitability performance. The Chi-square test supports that the difference across policy types is statistically significant and not just a visual pattern.

title: Executive Summary
text:
7. Profitability Trend Over Time

Key insight:

Average loss ratio increased from 0.67 in 2022
To 0.73 in 2023
To 0.87 in 2024
Still below break-even point of 1.00, but moving closer


The portfolio is still profitable on average because the loss ratio remains below 1.00. However, the upward trend is a warning sign. Average loss ratio increased from 0.67 in 2022 to 0.87 in 2024, meaning a larger share of premium is being used to cover incurred claims. Pairwise Wilcoxon tests show that loss ratio differs significantly across all year pairs, with adjusted p-values below 0.001. This suggests that profitability has weakened meaningfully over time.

title: Executive Summary
text:
8. Business Type and Underwriting Profit

Key insight:

Portfolio policies show higher underwriting profit than New Business policies
Wilcoxon test confirms significant difference: p < 0.001
Existing policies may be more profitable than newly acquired policies


This slide compares underwriting profit between new business and existing portfolio policies. The finding suggests that portfolio policies perform better than new business policies. This may happen because existing policies have more stable risk profiles, better pricing history or improved renewal selection. The Wilcoxon test confirms that the difference is statistically significant. For the insurer, this means acquisition growth should be monitored carefully to ensure that new business is not weakening overall profitability.

title: Executive Summary
text:
9. Bonus Score and Underwriting Profit

Key insight:

Good bonus score dominates the portfolio at 96.5%
Underwriting profit differs significantly across bonus score groups
Kruskal-Wallis result: H(2) = 977.21, p < 0.001
Bad group shows highest median profit, but group size is small


This finding is interesting because it is counterintuitive. We might expect better bonus scores to always show higher profitability, but the Bad group shows the highest median underwriting profit. However, this should not be over-interpreted because the Bad group is very small compared with the Good group. The result may be affected by pricing, coverage mix or small-group effects. The statistical test shows that the groups differ significantly, but further investigation is needed before making business decisions.

title: Executive Summary
text:
10. Claim Frequency

Key insight:

301,814 policies (85.7%) have no claims
17,911 policies (5.1%) have low claim frequency
32,565 policies (9.2%) have high claim frequency


Claim frequency is also zero-heavy, which is normal for motor insurance because most policyholders do not make claims in a given period. The majority of policies fall under the no-claim group. However, the high claim frequency group still matters because repeated claims can create volatility and may signal riskier behaviour or exposure. This slide helps separate claim occurrence from claim size, which is important because profitability pressure can come from either frequent claims or severe claims.

title: Executive Summary
text:
11. Claim Severity

Key insight:

Claim severity is strongly right-skewed
Median severity is around 498
Mean severity is higher at around 849
Standard deviation is around 2,936


Claim severity is the main volatility concern. The distribution is strongly right-skewed, meaning most claims are relatively small, but a small number of expensive claims pull the mean above the median. The high standard deviation also shows that claim costs vary widely. This matters because even if most policies have no claims, a few severe claims can still affect profitability. Therefore, the insurer should investigate high-severity claims in more detail using claim-level data.

title: Executive Summary
text:
12. Recommendations and Conclusion
Recommendations:

Review comprehensive without excess (COMP_N) policies due to higher loss-making share
Investigate why loss ratio increased from 2022 to 2024
Monitor New Business profitability against Portfolio policies
Investigate the Bad bonus score anomaly
Analyse high-severity claims using more granular claim-level data

Conclusion:
The portfolio remains profitable, but rising loss ratio suggests emerging profitability pressure.

Overall, the portfolio is still profitable, but the rising loss ratio suggests that profitability pressure is emerging. Policy type, business type, bonus score and year show meaningful relationships with profitability. Claim severity appears to be the main source of volatility because a small number of expensive claims can pull average claim cost upward. The insurer should prioritise reviewing COMP_N policies, understanding the worsening loss ratio trend and studying high-severity claims in more detail.

The propagation timeline shows that the instruction files remained active in the system for different lengths of time before the SaidIT post occurred. HiddenOrca and MellowOtter had short propagation windows of 2 days and 1 day respectively, while SwiftWren remained active for 8 days before the final post.
This suggests that the anomalous posts were not immediate one-step actions, but the result of file-based instructions circulating through the agent network over time. SwiftWren is the most concerning case because it had the longest observed propagation window before the post was executed.








ImportantMeaning and Probable Content



The anomalous SaidIT post does not appear to be meaningful human communication. It is best interpreted as a system artefact produced when John Windward’s agent treated file-based content as valid SaidIT post content.
The probable content of the post came from SwiftWren.txt, because the saidit_post event references this file as the content_source. However, the exact text inside SwiftWren.txt is not visible in the available event fields, so the precise gibberish content cannot be recovered directly.
The origin of the content is therefore inferred as file-based and instruction-driven: SwiftWren_further_instructions.md circulated before the post, the task was passed through the agent chain, SwiftWren.txt was used as the post source, and both related files were deleted after posting.

Each of the three file-sourced posts follows a similar structural pattern: an instruction file is passed through an agent delegation chain to John Windward’s agent, which then posts to SaidIT using a paired content file and deletes the related files afterwards.
The incident summary below is mostly derived from the event log. The post dates, content files, instruction files, poster, and deletion flags are computed from the data, while the delegation-chain labels are manually consolidated from the reconstructed event-chain evidence.

  filter(short_name == "saidit_post") %>%
  mutate(
    Content_file = str_match(
      details_text,
      '"content_source"\\s*:\\s*"([^"]+)"'
    )[, 2],
    Incident_file = str_remove(Content_file, "\\.txt$"),
    Instruction_file = paste0(Incident_file, "_further_instructions.md"),
    Date = as.Date(datetime),
    poster = str_extract(parties_text, "(?<=person:)[a-z_]+")

  filter(
    Incident_file %in% c("HiddenOrca", "MellowOtter", "SwiftWren")
  ) %>%

    post_id = id,
    post_row = row_order,
    Incident_file,
    Date,
    poster,
    Instruction_file,
    Content_file,
    details_text
  ) %>%
  arrange(Date)

# Step 2: extract all delete_file events

  filter(short_name == "delete_file") %>%
  select(
    delete_id = id,
    delete_row = row_order,
    delete_datetime = datetime,
    delete_details = details_text,
    delete_parties = parties_text

      delete_events$delete_row > post_row &
        delete_events$delete_row <= post_row + 50 &
        str_detect(delete_events$delete_details, fixed(Content_file))
    ),
    instruction_file_deleted = any(
      delete_events$delete_row > post_row &
        delete_events$delete_row <= post_row + 50 &
        str_detect(delete_events$delete_details, fixed(Instruction_file))

    Files_deleted_after = case_when(
      content_file_deleted & instruction_file_deleted ~ "Yes (both)",
      content_file_deleted | instruction_file_deleted ~ "Partial",
      TRUE ~ "No"
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    Incident = case_when(
      Incident_file == "SwiftWren" ~ "Incident 3 (target)",
      TRUE ~ paste0("Incident ", row_number())
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    Incident,
    Date,
    Instruction_file,
    Content_file,
    poster,
    Files_deleted_after,
    post_id,
    post_row
  )

    Chain_hops,
    Files_deleted_after
  )

    )

In the provided event log, this delegated further-instruction pattern is strongly associated with the suspicious incident chains. Therefore, the gate is precise: it targets the mechanism that allowed the instruction files to propagate across agents, while leaving normal email access, ordinary file access, and most agent delegation activity unaffected.
The high-volume anomalous/system-generated delegation category should be treated as a separate system issue. It may require independent investigation, but it is not the intervention point selected for this incident.

  ),

NoteWhy this intervention is effective



The Instruction Propagation Gate is effective for three reasons.
Precision: The gate does not block all delegation or all file access. It only pauses delegated read_file tasks involving _further_instructions.md files, which were strongly associated with the suspicious chains in the provided event log.
Early detection: The instruction files appeared before the final SaidIT posts. Pausing the chain at the delegated file-reading stage gives administrators time to investigate before the content is posted externally.
Coverage: The gate does not need to know which agent will eventually execute the post. It triggers on the file-propagation pattern itself, which means it can catch future variants even if the upstream delegation path changes.

7.2 Why the Post Appeared as Gibberish: A Size Comparison
The post likely appeared as gibberish because the content file was much larger than a normal SaidIT post. Instead of posting a short readable message, the system treated a large file as the message content. The chart below compares the size of each incident content file against the normal SaidIT post content length range.


Show the code
# Helper function to extract file size from available event fields
extract_size_num <- function(x) {
  size_hint <- str_match(x, '"size_hint"\\s*:\\s*([0-9]+)')[, 2]
  content_length <- str_match(x, '"content_length"\\s*:\\s*([0-9]+)')[, 2]
  suppressWarnings(as.numeric(coalesce(size_hint, content_length)))
}

# Normal post content lengths from the event log
normal_posts <- events %>%
  filter(
    short_name == "saidit_post",
    !str_detect(details_text, '"content_source"')
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    content = str_match(details_text, '"content":"([^"]+)"')[, 2],
    content_len = nchar(content)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(content_len))

normal_stats <- normal_posts %>%
  summarise(
    min_len = min(content_len),
    max_len = max(content_len),
    avg_len = mean(content_len)
  )

avg_normal <- normal_stats$avg_len[1]

# Incident file sizes derived from the event log
incident_file_sizes <- events %>%
  mutate(
    content_file = str_extract(
      details_text,
      "(HiddenOrca|MellowOtter|SwiftWren)\\.txt"
    ),
    size_bytes = extract_size_num(details_text)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(content_file)) %>%
  group_by(content_file) %>%
  summarise(
    size_bytes = {
      vals <- size_bytes[!is.na(size_bytes)]
      if (length(vals) == 0) NA_real_ else max(vals)
    },
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    label = case_when(
      content_file == "SwiftWren.txt" ~ "SwiftWren.txt\n(Incident 3)",
      content_file == "MellowOtter.txt" ~ "MellowOtter.txt\n(Incident 2)",
      content_file == "HiddenOrca.txt" ~ "HiddenOrca.txt\n(Incident 1)"
    ),
    type = if_else(
      is.na(size_bytes),
      "Incident file (size unknown)",
      "Incident file"
    )
  )

swift_size <- incident_file_sizes %>%
  filter(content_file == "SwiftWren.txt") %>%
  pull(size_bytes) %>%
  first()

mellow_size <- incident_file_sizes %>%
  filter(content_file == "MellowOtter.txt") %>%
  pull(size_bytes) %>%
  first()

swift_mult <- round(swift_size / avg_normal)
mellow_mult <- round(mellow_size / avg_normal)

# Comparison bar chart
comparison_df <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    label = paste0("Normal SaidIT post\n(avg ", round(avg_normal), " chars)"),
    size_bytes = avg_normal,
    type = "Normal post"
  ),
  incident_file_sizes %>%
    filter(!is.na(size_bytes)) %>%
    select(label, size_bytes, type)
) %>%
  mutate(
    label = factor(label, levels = rev(label)),
    fill_col = if_else(type == "Normal post", "#457b9d", "#e63946"),
    size_label = if_else(
      type == "Normal post",
      paste0(round(size_bytes), " chars"),
      paste0(
        scales::comma(round(size_bytes)),
        " bytes\n(~",
        round(size_bytes / avg_normal),
        "x a normal post)"
      )
    )
  )

ggplot(comparison_df, aes(x = label, y = size_bytes, fill = fill_col)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = size_label),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 3.2,
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.45)),
    labels = scales::comma
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Content File Size vs Normal SaidIT Post Length",
    subtitle = "Incident files were hundreds of times larger than a normal SaidIT message",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Size (bytes / characters)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )















NoteObservations



A normal SaidIT post in this system is between 37 and 96 characters, with an average length of about 60 characters.
By comparison, SwiftWren.txt was 30,615 bytes, about 509 times larger than a normal post. MellowOtter.txt was even larger at 44,879 bytes, about 747 times larger than a normal post.
